unit.title: AI security policy and red teaming at school

lesson.title: A policy that holds
lesson.subtitle: Rules people can follow, checks systems enforce

video.title: A policy that holds
video.format_note: Animated explainer, 16:9, flat Darsi colours on paper-grey backgrounds, one recurring teacher character. Narration in the lesson language; captions as separate files, never burned in.
cast: Dr Farah Rahman — university lecturer in education, Bangladesh (main character)
Mr Joseph Mwangi — computer studies teacher, Kenya (cameo)
Narrator — the Darsi voice (warm, peer to peer)

scenes.visual: Cards: Twelve careful pages; Read by no one; Protects nobody.
scenes.animation: Each item arrives as it is said.
scenes.narration: I once read a school's AI policy. Twelve pages, careful and complete, and not one teacher had read it. A policy that nobody follows protects nobody.

scenes.visual: The title card: the course, the lesson title and subtitle, the Darsi mark.
scenes.animation: Mark pops in; the title slides up.
scenes.narration: Today: an AI security policy on one page, and how to turn its rules into checks that hold.

scenes.visual: A list: Approved tools, and how to add one; Data rules: green, amber, red; What needs a person's yes; Detectors, fakes, reporting.
scenes.animation: Each item arrives as it is said.
scenes.narration: A good AI security policy fits on one page. It says which tools are approved, and how a new one gets approved. It sets the data rules: green, amber and red. It says what agents may do alone, and what needs a person's yes. And it covers detectors, fakes and how to report a problem.

scenes.visual: A list: Where does our data go?; What age does it allow?; What can it do alone?; Who looks after it?.
scenes.animation: Each item arrives as it is said.
scenes.narration: Approving a tool means asking a few questions first. Where does our data go, and is it used for training? What age does it allow? What can it do on its own? And who will look after it here?

scenes.visual: Two columns. A rule to remember: “Please ask first”; Forgotten on busy days. A check that's enforced: No send without a yes; Holds every day; A setting or code.
scenes.animation: Each item arrives as it is said.
scenes.narration: Here's what makes a policy hold. A rule people must remember will be forgotten on a busy day. A check the system enforces holds every day. So wherever you can, turn the rule into a setting, a permission or a line of code.

scenes.animation: Each item arrives as it is said.
scenes.narration: Here's our send rule as code, with a bug we found in it. The first version sent a message if the agent asked or a teacher said yes, so the agent could approve itself. One word fixes it: and, instead of or. Now it sends only when both are true, every single time.

scenes.visual: The quick check: the question and its answer cards, with the speaker beside them.
scenes.animation: The speaker slides in; answer cards drop in.
scenes.narration: Quick check! Two schools want the same thing: no messages to parents without a teacher's yes. Which rule holds?

scenes.visual: Cards: Tap Approve to send; Holds every day; Posters: for habits; Like taking names out.
scenes.animation: Each item arrives as it is said.
scenes.narration: The second. When the bot simply can't send without a tap on Approve, the rule holds on the busiest day. Keep posters for habits only people can do, like taking names out of a prompt.

scenes.visual: A list: In your community's languages; Check your data protection law; Review each term; And after an incident.
scenes.animation: Each item arrives as it is said.
scenes.narration: Write the page in plain words, in the languages your staff, pupils and parents read. Check it against your country's data protection law. Then review it each term, and whenever a new tool or an incident arrives.

scenes.visual: Cards joined by arrows: Pick a job; Grant tools; Count the damage; Only what's needed.
scenes.animation: Each item arrives as it is said.
scenes.on_screen_text: App lab: only what it needs
scenes.narration: In the app, pick a job and give an agent its tools. Run the attack set and count the damage. Then cut the tools to what the job needs and run it again: that list of tools is a line in your policy.

scenes.visual: The quick check: the question and its answer cards, with the speaker beside them.
scenes.animation: The speaker slides in; answer cards drop in.
scenes.narration: Your turn. Our timetable agent only needs to read the timetable, but it was given email too. What should the policy say?

scenes.visual: The summary: One page, plain words; Questions before approval; Checks the system enforces; Review each term. Takeaway: If it matters, make the system enforce it.
scenes.animation: Points tick in as they are said; the takeaway slides up.
scenes.narration: Only the tools its job needs. Remember: one page in plain words, questions before a tool is approved, checks the system enforces, and a review each term.

scenes.visual: A list: Two colleagues, two pupils; Draft one page; Remember or enforce?; One rule into a setting.
scenes.animation: Each item arrives as it is said.
scenes.on_screen_text: Try it at school this week
scenes.narration: Try it at school this week: draft your one-page policy with two colleagues and two pupils. Mark each rule: something people remember, or something the system enforces. Then turn one rule into a setting this week.

checkpoints.prompt: Two schools want no messages to parents without a teacher's yes. Which rule holds?

options.text: A poster: “Always check before the bot sends”
The bot can't send until a teacher taps Approve
A reminder at every staff meeting

checkpoints.feedback_correct: Yes: the system enforces it, even on a busy day.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite: posters and reminders get forgotten. A check in the system holds.

checkpoints.prompt: The timetable agent only needs to read the timetable, but it was given email too. What should the policy say?

options.text: Keep email: it might be useful one day
Each agent gets only the tools its job needs
Agents may use any tool, if they are polite

checkpoints.feedback_correct: Yes: least privilege. Take email away and the agent can't be tricked into sending.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite: every extra tool is something an attack could use. Give only what the job needs.
